messages.content: Translate this business email into German, keeping it formal: "Dear Ms. Berger, Due to a delay at our supplier, delivery of your order will be postponed by one week. The new delivery date is March 14. We apologize for the inconvenience and will keep you informed."

Sehr geehrte Frau Berger,

aufgrund einer Verzögerung bei unserem Lieferanten verschiebt sich die Lieferung Ihrer Bestellung um eine Woche. Der neue Liefertermin ist der 14. März. Wir entschuldigen uns für die Unannehmlichkeiten und werden Sie weiterhin auf dem Laufenden halten.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen

Two register notes: a German business email opens with «Sehr geehrte Frau Berger» and closes with «Mit freundlichen Grüßen» — there is no equivalent of a casual sign-off in this context. And «wir entschuldigen uns für...» is the standard apology formula; «es tut uns leid» is a shade warmer and also acceptable.
Guten Abend! Ich habe ein Zimmer auf den Namen Weber reserviert. Ist es möglich, ein ruhiges Zimmer zu bekommen?
Guten Abend, Frau Weber! Ja, natürlich. Ich gebe Ihnen ein Zimmer im dritten Stock, weg von der Straße. Das Frühstück gibt es von 7 bis 10 Uhr im Erdgeschoss.
Vielen Dank! Könnten Sie mir noch das WLAN-Passwort geben?
Gern. Das Passwort lautet «HotelSonne2026». Der Empfang ist rund um die Uhr besetzt — wenn Sie etwas brauchen, rufen Sie einfach die 9 an. Ich wünsche Ihnen einen angenehmen Aufenthalt!
When do I use «Sie» and when «du» in German? My course teaches both but never says how to choose, and I'm terrified of insulting someone.

A safe default: use «Sie» with every adult you don't know — officials, shop staff, doctors, older people, and anyone in a professional setting. «Sie» can never really insult; at worst it sounds a little stiff.

«Du» is for friends, family, children, fellow students, and increasingly for colleagues in younger or creative workplaces. Many startups and sports clubs use «du» from day one.

The tricky part is switching. Traditionally the older or higher-ranking person offers it: «Wir können uns gern duzen» (we can use du, if you like). If someone offers, accept — refusing would be awkward. And if you're unsure with a colleague, just follow their lead: if they address you with «du», answer with «du».

Note the verb forms differ: «Sie haben / Sie sind» versus «du hast / du bist». Mixing «du» with a Sie-form verb is the one combination that really sounds wrong.

Translate these safety instructions into German for a product manual: "Warning: Disconnect the device from the power supply before opening the housing. Do not operate the device with wet hands. Keep away from children."

Warnung: Trennen Sie das Gerät vor dem Öffnen des Gehäuses von der Stromversorgung. Bedienen Sie das Gerät nicht mit nassen Händen. Außer Reichweite von Kindern aufbewahren.

Manual style notes: German instructions address the user with the formal «Sie» imperative («Trennen Sie...», «Bedienen Sie...»). You will also see the infinitive style on packaging — «Vor dem Öffnen vom Netz trennen» — which is even more compressed and impersonal. Both are correct; the Sie-form is clearer for a full manual. «Stromversorgung» (power supply) is the technical term; «Stecker ziehen» would be the everyday version.
Correct my German: "Ich habe Interesse für die Wohnung und ich möchte wissen, ob sie ist noch frei."

Two errors:

1. «Interesse für» → «Interesse an» (+ dative). The fixed phrase is «Interesse an etwas haben»: «Ich habe Interesse an der Wohnung.»

2. Word order in the subordinate clause. After «ob», the verb goes to the very end: «ob sie noch frei ist», not «ob sie ist noch frei».

Corrected: «Ich habe Interesse an der Wohnung und ich möchte wissen, ob sie noch frei ist.»
Guten Tag, ich rufe wegen der Wohnung in der Goethestraße an. Ist sie noch frei?
Guten Tag! Ja, die Wohnung ist noch frei. Möchten Sie einen Besichtigungstermin vereinbaren?
Sehr gern. Können Sie mir vorher sagen, wie hoch die Nebenkosten und die Kaution sind?
Die Nebenkosten betragen 180 Euro im Monat, und die Kaution ist drei Monatsmieten, also 2.700 Euro. Einzug wäre ab dem 1. Dezember möglich. Passt Ihnen ein Termin am Donnerstag um 17 Uhr?
Why do Germans say «Ich hätte gern ein Bier» instead of «Ich will ein Bier»? What is this «hätte» form doing?

«Hätte» is the Konjunktiv II (subjunctive) of «haben», and its job here is pure politeness. Compare:

- «Ich will ein Bier» — I want a beer. Grammatically fine, socially blunt; it sounds like a demand.
- «Ich möchte ein Bier» — I would like a beer. «Möchte» is already a softened subjunctive form.
- «Ich hätte gern ein Bier» — literally "I would have gladly a beer"; the standard, friendly way to order.

The same pattern appears everywhere in polite German:
- «Könnten Sie mir helfen?» — Could you help me? (instead of «Können Sie...?»)
- «Wäre es möglich, später zu kommen?» — Would it be possible to come later?
- «Ich würde gern zahlen.» — I'd like to pay, please.

Rule of thumb: the subjunctive wraps the request in a small hypothetical — "if it were possible" — and that distance is exactly what makes it polite.
Translate this product description into natural English: «Dieser Rucksack aus wasserabweisendem Material bietet 25 Liter Volumen, ein gepolstertes Laptopfach und verstellbare Schultergurte.»

"Made from water-repellent fabric, this backpack offers a 25-litre capacity, a padded laptop compartment, and adjustable shoulder straps."

Two translation choices: «wasserabweisend» is "water-repellent", not "waterproof" — German distinguishes the two carefully («wasserdicht» would be fully waterproof), and overstating it in English could mislead buyers. And German product copy loves the verb «bieten» (to offer); English sounds more natural when the features simply become the subject, as above.
Correct this sentence: "Wegen dem schlechten Wetter sind wir zu Hause geblieben." A native speaker told me something is off.

In standard written German, «wegen» takes the genitive: «Wegen des schlechten Wetters sind wir zu Hause geblieben.»

Your version, «wegen dem...», is extremely common in everyday speech — you will hear it constantly, and nobody will misunderstand you. But in exams, formal writing, and careful speech it is marked as wrong. The same applies to «trotz» (despite): «trotz des Regens», not «trotz dem Regen».

A useful escape hatch: «aufgrund des schlechten Wetters» or simply «weil das Wetter so schlecht war» sidesteps the case question entirely.
How am I supposed to read a monster word like «Geschwindigkeitsbegrenzung»? German words seem endless.

Break it from the right. German compounds are built backwards: the last part is the actual thing, everything before it just describes it.

Geschwindigkeits-begrenzung:
- die Begrenzung = the limit (this is the head — it gives the word its gender and plural)
- die Geschwindigkeit = speed
- the extra «-s-» is a linking sound (Fugen-s) that glues the parts together

So: a "speed-limit" — a speed limit sign, in fact.

Same trick with «Handschuhfach»: Fach (compartment) + Schuh (shoe) + Hand (hand) = the "hand-shoe compartment" — a glove box. Once you start spotting the head noun at the end, even very long words fall apart into small familiar pieces.

Translate this complaint email into German — polite but firm: "Dear Sir or Madam, I stayed in room 204 from November 20 to 22. The room was very noisy at night and had not been cleaned properly on arrival. I would like a partial refund of one night's charge. Please let me know how you will resolve this."

Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,

ich war vom 20. bis 22. November Gast in Ihrem Haus (Zimmer 204). Leider war das Zimmer nachts sehr laut und bei meiner Ankunft nicht ordentlich gereinigt. Ich bitte Sie daher um eine teilweise Rückerstattung in Höhe einer Übernachtung. Bitte teilen Sie mir mit, wie Sie diese Angelegenheit regeln werden.

Mit freundlichen Grüßen

Note the firm-but-correct tone: German complaints state facts and a concrete request («Ich bitte Sie daher um...») rather than expressing anger. «Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren» is the standard opening when you don't have a name — never «Hallo» in a written complaint.
Guten Tag, ich bin neu in Berlin und muss mich anmelden. Was brauche ich dafür?
Guten Tag! Für die Anmeldung brauche ich Ihren Reisepass und die Wohnungsgeberbestätigung von Ihrem Vermieter. Haben Sie beides dabei?
Ja, hier sind mein Pass und das Formular vom Vermieter.

Alles in Ordnung, danke. Einen Moment bitte... Hier ist Ihre Meldebescheinigung. Bewahren Sie sie gut auf — Sie brauchen sie zum Beispiel für ein Bankkonto oder einen Handyvertrag. Einen schönen Tag noch!
What's the difference between «kennen» and «wissen»? Both seem to mean "to know".

They divide the territory that English gives to one verb:

«Kennen» = to be familiar with a person, place, or thing (knowledge by acquaintance):
- «Ich kenne Berlin gut.» — I know Berlin well.
- «Kennst du diesen Film?» — Do you know this film?

«Wissen» = to know a fact, usually followed by a clause or a question word:
- «Ich weiß, dass der Zug um 9 Uhr fährt.» — I know that the train leaves at 9.
- «Weißt du, wo der Bahnhof ist?» — Do you know where the station is?

Quick test: if you can replace "know" with "be familiar with", use «kennen». If what follows is a fact, a «dass»-clause, or a question word (wo, wann, ob, wie), use «wissen».

Translate the opening of my cover letter into German: "Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing to apply for the position of software developer advertised on your website. I have five years of experience in backend development and would welcome the opportunity to discuss my application in person."

Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren,

mit großem Interesse habe ich Ihre Stellenanzeige auf Ihrer Website gelesen und bewerbe mich hiermit um die Position als Softwareentwickler. Ich verfüge über fünf Jahre Erfahrung in der Backend-Entwicklung und würde mich über die Gelegenheit freuen, meine Bewerbung in einem persönlichen Gespräch zu erläutern.

German cover letters rarely translate "I am writing to apply" word for word. The conventional opening is «mit großem Interesse habe ich Ihre Stellenanzeige gelesen und bewerbe mich hiermit um...» — it sounds formulaic because it is: German recruiters expect exactly these formulas, and originality is saved for the body of the letter.
Correct my German: "Er hat mich geholfen und den Koffer getragen."

One error: «helfen» takes the dative, not the accusative. It must be «Er hat mir geholfen und den Koffer getragen.» (He helped me and carried the suitcase.)

«Helfen» belongs to a small group of common verbs that govern the dative: helfen (to help), danken (to thank), folgen (to follow), gefallen (to please), gehören (to belong to). English speakers trip over these because English uses a direct object for all of them — "he helped me" — but German asks "helped to-me": «Er hat mir gedankt» = he thanked me.
Es regnet schon wieder! Ich hoffe, am Wochenende wird das Wetter besser. Wir wollen in die Berge fahren.
Ich drücke die Daumen! Laut Wetterbericht soll es am Samstag sonnig werden. Fahrt ihr zum Wandern oder nur für einen Tagesausflug?
Wir wandern auf die Zugspitze — na ja, wir nehmen die Seilbahn nach oben und wandern dann ein bisschen.
Das klingt nach einem guten Plan! Die Aussicht von oben ist fantastisch, wenn keine Wolken da sind. Vergesst die warmen Jacken nicht — oben ist es auch im Sommer kalt.
When do I write ß and when ss in German? Straße has ß, but Wasser has ss, and I can't see the pattern.

The pattern is vowel length:

- After a LONG vowel or a diphthong, write ß: Straße (long a), groß (long o), weiß (diphthong ei), heißen.
- After a SHORT vowel, write ss: Wasser (short a), muss (short u), Kuss, Fluss.

So the spelling actually tells you how to pronounce the word: ß means "stretch the vowel before me", ss means "clip it short".

Two extras: Switzerland doesn't use ß at all — Swiss German writes Strasse, gross. And since 2017 there is an official capital ẞ, though most people still write STRASSE in all-caps.
Translate into German: "The bridge was built in 1902 and is still used by thousands of people every day."

«Die Brücke wurde 1902 gebaut und wird noch heute jeden Tag von Tausenden von Menschen benutzt.»

German uses two different passive forms here, and the tense does the work:
- «wurde gebaut» — the werden-passive in the past: the building happened once, in 1902.
- «wird benutzt» — the same passive in the present: the using is still going on.

The agent («by thousands of people») is introduced with «von» + dative: «von Tausenden von Menschen». English speakers often reach for «durch» here, but «durch» is for the means or channel (durch die Presse bekannt), not for the doer.
Why does «Ich rufe dich morgen an» have that little «an» stranded at the end? Where did it come from?

It comes from the verb itself: «anrufen» (to phone) is a separable verb. In a main clause it splits in two — the verb stem goes to position two, and the prefix is kicked to the end of the sentence:

- anrufen → «Ich rufe dich morgen an.»
- aufstehen → «Ich stehe um 7 Uhr auf.» (I get up at 7.)
- einkaufen → «Wir kaufen heute ein.» (We're shopping today.)

The good news: in a subordinate clause the verb stays in one piece at the end, so the prefix comes home: «..., weil ich dich morgen anrufe.»

When you learn a new verb, always check whether it's separable (dictionaries mark it, and the prefix is always stressed: ÁNrufen). The meaning often changes completely — «rufen» alone means to shout or call out, not to phone.
Guten Tag, ich möchte gern einen Tisch für Samstagabend reservieren, für sechs Personen.
Guten Tag! Für Samstag habe ich noch einen Tisch um 19:30 Uhr frei. Auf welchen Namen darf ich reservieren?
Auf den Namen Hoffmann. Eine Frage: Haben Sie auch vegetarische Gerichte? Zwei von uns essen kein Fleisch.
Ja, wir haben mehrere vegetarische Hauptgerichte und auch eine vegane Option. Ich notiere das gleich mit. Dann bis Samstag, Frau Hoffmann — wir freuen uns auf Sie!

Translate this business email into Chinese: "Dear Mr. Wang, Thank you for your quotation. Could you please send us the updated price list before Friday? We would also like to arrange a video call next week to discuss the contract terms."

尊敬的王先生：

您好！感谢您的报价。请您在本周五之前将最新价格表发给我们。另外，我们希望下周安排一次视频会议，讨论合同条款。

期待您的回复，顺祝商祺！

Register notes: Chinese business emails open with «尊敬的» (respected) before the name and title, and a common sign-off is «顺祝商祺» — a formulaic wish for commercial good fortune that has no English equivalent; "best regards" is its functional match. Deadlines are stated plainly with «在……之前» (before...), which is polite without being soft.
I keep seeing this sign in restaurants: 欢迎光临，请问几位？ Can you tell me what it says and how to pronounce it?

It says: 欢迎光临，请问几位？
Pinyin: Huānyíng guānglín, qǐngwèn jǐ wèi?
Meaning: "Welcome! May I ask, how many people (in your party)?"

Breakdown:
- 欢迎 (huānyíng) — welcome
- 光临 (guānglín) — your gracious arrival; a polite, shop-style word for a customer coming in
- 请问 (qǐngwèn) — "may I ask", the standard polite opener for a question
- 几位 (jǐ wèi) — how many people, using 位, the polite measure word for people

So when you walk into a restaurant in China and hear this, the expected answer is just a number: 两位 (liǎng wèi) — two of us.
你好，我要办理登机手续。这是我的护照。我可以要一个靠窗的座位吗？
好的，没问题。靠窗的座位还有。请问您有托运行李吗？
有一个行李箱要托运。免费托运的限额是多少公斤？
经济舱免费托运限额是二十公斤，您的箱子是十八公斤，没有超重。这是您的登机牌，登机口是十二号，三点四十分开始登机。祝您旅途愉快！
Correct my Chinese: 我被他把钱包偷走了。Something feels tangled.

Your instinct is right — you've stacked the 被 (bèi) passive and the 把 (bǎ) construction on top of each other, and Chinese makes you choose one frame:

1. 被 passive (focus on you, the victim): 我的钱包被他偷走了。— My wallet was stolen by him.
2. 把 construction (focus on what he did with the wallet): 他把我的钱包偷走了。— He took my wallet (and it's gone).

Both are correct and common. The mix «我被他把……» forces the listener to process two competing sentence frames at once, so it breaks down. Pick the frame that matches what you want to emphasize: the sufferer (被） or the thing disposed of （把）.
的, 地, 得 — they all sound like "de" and I use them randomly. Is there an actual system?

There is, and it's purely positional. All three are pronounced with a neutral tone, but each has one job:

1. 的 before a NOUN (possession or description): 我的书 (my book), 红色的花 (a red flower), 他写的信 (the letter he wrote).
2. 地 before a VERB (turns an adjective into an adverb): 慢慢地走 (walk slowly), 高兴地说 (say happily).
3. 得 after a VERB or adjective (introduces a degree or result): 跑得快 (run fast — literally "run to the extent of fast"), 好得不得了 (incredibly good).

Memory hook: 的 hugs nouns, 地 launches verbs, 得 trails behind them. In handwriting and exams the distinction matters; in speech nobody can hear it anyway.
Translate these product instructions into English: 使用前请仔细阅读说明书。本产品不防水，请勿在浴室使用。充电时间为两小时。

"Please read the instruction manual carefully before use. This product is not waterproof; do not use it in the bathroom. Charging time is two hours."

A few fixed expressions worth knowing, because they appear on almost every Chinese product: 使用前 (before use), 请仔细阅读 (please read carefully), 请勿 (do not — the formal, written cousin of 不要）, and 说明书 (instruction manual, literally "explanation book"). Once you recognize 请勿， warning labels everywhere become readable.
At a dinner in Chengdu someone told me 入乡随俗 when I hesitated over the spicy food. What does it mean?

入乡随俗 (rù xiāng suí sú) means "when you enter a village, follow its customs" — the Chinese equivalent of "when in Rome, do as the Romans do."

Character by character:
- 入 (rù) — to enter
- 乡 (xiāng) — village, hometown
- 随 (suí) — to follow
- 俗 (sú) — customs, local ways

Your host was being kind, not critical: the phrase is a gentle nudge that adapting to local habits — including bravely eating the hotpot — is the respectful and smart move. You can also use it about yourself: 我入乡随俗，吃了火锅。 (I did as the locals do and ate the hotpot.)
你好，我想看看这款手机。它保修几年？
您好，这款手机全国联保两年，屏幕和电池都在保修范围内。您想看黑色还是白色？
黑色的。价格还能便宜一点吗？有点贵。
这样吧，今天店里有活动，我给您便宜一百块，再送一个手机壳和一张贴膜。您看怎么样？
I tried to tell a street vendor I wanted to BUY dumplings and he looked confused, then laughed. My tones must be off. What's happening?

You've hit the most famous tone trap in Chinese:

- 买 (mǎi, third tone — the dipping tone) = to BUY
- 卖 (mài, fourth tone — the sharp falling tone) = to SELL

Same sounds, opposite directions of money. If your third tone comes out flat or falling, the vendor hears a stranger announcing he wants to sell dumplings.

The dumpling pair is even better:
- 水饺 (shuǐjiǎo) = boiled dumplings
- 睡觉 (shuìjiào) = to sleep

Ask for shuìjiào and you're asking to sleep. Practice tip: exaggerate the third tone's dip — go down, then come back up, like a small valley. Native speakers forgive almost every tone error except this pair, purely because the misunderstanding is so funny.
Translate this station announcement notice into Chinese: "Please keep your belongings with you at all times. Unattended bags will be removed for security reasons."

请随身携带好您的物品。出于安全考虑，无人看管的行李将被移除。

(Pinyin for reading it aloud: Qǐng suíshēn xiédài hǎo nín de wùpǐn. Chūyú ānquán kǎolǜ, wúrén kānguǎn de xíngli jiāng bèi yíchú.)

Notice the formal devices: 随身携带 (carry on your person) instead of the everyday 带着， the polite 您 for "your", and the passive 将被 (will be) — written announcements in Chinese prefer this bookish passive over the spoken 被 alone.
I keep meeting verb pairs like 看懂, 听清楚, 做完, 找到. They look like two verbs glued together. What are they?

They're resultative complements: verb + result. The first character is the action, the second is the outcome the action reaches:

- 看懂 (kàn-dǒng) — read/look UNTIL you understand: 看 is the looking, 懂 (understand) is the result
- 听清楚 (tīng-qīngchu) — listen until it's clear
- 做完 (zuò-wán) — do until finished
- 找到 (zhǎo-dào) — search until found

This is why Chinese often needs two syllables where English needs an adverb or a whole phrase. Crucially, they have a potential form with 得/不 in the middle: 看得懂 (able to understand by reading) vs 看不懂 (can't understand it no matter how much I read). «我听不懂» — I can't make out what I'm hearing — is probably the single most useful sentence a learner owns.
I need to decline a colleague's dinner invitation on WeChat — I have a family thing, but I want to stay friendly and suggest next time. Can you write the message in Chinese?

Here's a message that hits the warm-but-clear tone WeChat refusals need:

不好意思啊，我今晚家里有点事，实在去不了。你们吃得开心点！下次我请客，咱们再约。

(Bù hǎoyìsi a, wǒ jīnwǎn jiā lǐ yǒu diǎn shì, shízài qù bù liǎo. Nǐmen chī de kāixīn diǎn! Xià cì wǒ qǐngkè, zánmen zài yuē.)

Why it works: 不好意思啊 softens the opening; 实在去不了 (really can't make it) makes the refusal firm without a long excuse; and 下次我请客 (next time it's on me) turns the no into a future yes. Offering a specific alternative matters more in Chinese workplace culture than a detailed explanation of the conflict.
Correct my Chinese: 我们都学生是，所以我们每天都上课。

The problem is where 都 (dōu, all/both) sits. It must stand directly before the verb, not before the noun:

✗ 我们都学生是
✓ 我们都是学生，所以我们每天都上课。
(Wǒmen dōu shì xuéshēng, suǒyǐ wǒmen měitiān dōu shàngkè. — We are all students, so we have class every day.)

Notice your second 都 was already perfect: 每天都上课 — 都 right before 上课. The rule never changes: 都 always hugs the verb that follows it. «We all students are» is an English word-order transplant; Chinese wants «we all ARE students».
Translate this into English: 春节是中国最重要的传统节日。每年这个时候，不管多远，人们都会赶回家，和家人一起吃年夜饭。

"The Spring Festival is China's most important traditional holiday. Every year at this time, no matter how far away they are, people hurry home to eat the New Year's Eve dinner with their families."

One phrase deserves unpacking: 年夜饭 (niányèfàn) is literally the "year-night meal" — the reunion dinner eaten on the eve of the lunar new year. It isn't just a big dinner; it's the emotional center of the holiday, and the annual migration home for it （春运， the Spring Festival travel rush) is the largest recurring movement of people on Earth.
How do I read this date out loud in Chinese: 2026年11月26日，星期四？ And is there anything special about saying a phone number?

Read the date digit by digit for the year, then normally for the rest:

二零二六年十一月二十六日，星期四。
(Èr líng èr liù nián shíyī yuè èrshíliù rì, xīngqī sì.)
— November 26, 2026, Thursday.

Years are read as individual digits (2026 = 二零二六， "two zero two six"), unlike English "twenty twenty-six".

Phone numbers are also read digit by digit, with one famous twist: the digit 1 is pronounced yāo instead of yī, to avoid confusion with 7 (qī). So 138... starts yāo-sān-bā. You'll hear this in every phone number, taxi dispatch, and hotel room number in China.
你好，不好意思，可以帮我们拍张照片吗？
当然可以！你们站好，对，就站在这个牌子前面。好了，拍完了，你们看一下行不行。
拍得真好，谢谢你！你也是来旅游的吗？
是啊，我从西安过来，第一次来北京。你们呢？祝你们玩得开心，再见！
Why do I have to say 我把门关了 instead of just 我关门了？ Both seem to mean "I closed the door".

They're close, but 把 adds a meaning English hides: disposal — something was done TO the door, and it ended up in a new state.

- 我关门了。(Wǒ guān mén le.) — I closed the door. Neutral report of the action; also fine if you're just narrating.
- 我把门关了。(Wǒ bǎ mén guān le.) — I got the door closed. Focus on the door and its resulting state: shut, dealt with.

Two consequences: first, 把-sentences require the verb to carry a result — you can't say 我把门关 (bare verb, nothing after it); something like 了， 上， 好， or a complement must complete it. Second, 把 is chosen when the object is specific and affected: 我把信写好了 (I wrote the letter — done), 请把窗户打开 (please get the window open). If nothing is being "handled" or changed, plain word order is better.
This message is fine for my friend but I need to send almost the same thing to my professor. Casual version: 老王，我明天去你那儿拿东西，行吗？ Make it polite.

Polite version:

王老师，您好。我明天想去您办公室取一下东西，请问您方便吗？

(Wáng lǎoshī, nín hǎo. Wǒ míngtiān xiǎng qù nín bàngōngshì qǔ yíxià dōngxi, qǐngwèn nín fāngbiàn ma?)

What changed, piece by piece:
- 老王 (Old Wang — affectionate, for peers only) → 王老师 (Teacher Wang, the respectful address)
- 你 → 您 (nín, the polite "you") — used twice
- 你那儿 (your place) → 您办公室 (your office): the destination gets named respectfully
- 去拿东西 → 取一下东西： 取 is the slightly formal word for fetching, and 一下 softens the action ("just quickly grab")
- 行吗？ (ok?) → 请问您方便吗？ (may I ask whether it's convenient for you) — the question is reframed around the professor's convenience, not your plan

Same facts, completely different relationship.
Translate this business email into Japanese: "Thank you for your email. I have attached the revised quotation. Please let me know if you have any questions."

メールをありがとうございます。修正した見積書を添付いたします。ご不明な点がございましたら、お気軽にお知らせください。

(Meeru o arigatoo gozaimasu. Shuusei shita mitsumorisho o tenpu itashimasu. Go-fumei na ten ga gozaimashitara, okigaru ni oshirase kudasai.)

Business notes: «添付いたします» uses the humble form いたす because attaching is YOUR action toward the client. And questions are not «質問» here — the set phrase is «ご不明な点» (any unclear points), which sounds softer and more professional. Business emails also typically open with «お世話になっております» before anything else.
When do Japanese people use the plain form like 食べる instead of 食べます? If I always use ます-form, am I safe?

Mostly safe, yes — the ます-form will never offend anyone. But you will hear the plain (dictionary) form constantly, and understanding the switch matters:

Use ます-form with: strangers, shop staff, colleagues, anyone older or higher in status, and in all business settings.

Plain form appears with: close friends, family, younger people you know well, children — and in your own muttering to yourself. Written Japanese (novels, news, reports) also uses plain form as its neutral style.

The subtle part: Japanese speakers shift mid-relationship. When a colleague starts answering you in plain form, that's often a small signal of closeness — you can gradually mirror it. Staying in ます-form forever with friends sounds distant rather than polite, like calling a friend "sir" in English.

Grammar bonus: everything else in the sentence follows the final verb's register — if the verb is plain, sentence endings like だ and particles like よ/ね feel natural; mixing registers mid-sentence is what actually sounds odd.
Correct my Japanese: 私は図書館で本を読みましたかった。

Almost — the problem is where the past tense landed. It should be:

私は図書館で本を読みたかった。
(Watashi wa toshokan de hon o yomitakatta. — I wanted to read a book at the library.)

The ～たい (want to) ending attaches to the verb STEM (読み）, and ～たい itself conjugates like an i-adjective: 読みたい → 読みたかった (wanted to). The main verb never gets a past ending of its own in this pattern. Your version «読みましたかった» tried to stack ました-past under たい, which Japanese doesn't allow.

Same rule everywhere: 行きたい → 行きたかった (wanted to go), 食べたくない (don't want to eat).
すみません、チェックインをお願いします。予約したスミスです。
スミス様ですね、お待ちしておりました。お部屋は二階でございます。夕食は六時から八時まで、温泉は夜十一時までご利用いただけます。
ありがとうございます。朝ごはんは何時からですか。
朝食は七時からでございます。アレルギーなどございましたら、今お伺いしておきますが、いかがでしょうか。どうぞごゆっくりお過ごしくださいませ。
I'm at a restaurant in Kyoto and the sign says 禁煙席, and the menu has 刺身定食. Can you read these for me?

Both are worth learning whole:

1. 禁煙席 — きんえんせき (kin'enseki): "no-smoking seats". 禁 (kin, prohibit) + 煙 (en, smoke/tobacco) + 席 (seki, seat). You'll also see its opposite, 喫煙席 (kitsuenseki, smoking seats).

2. 刺身定食 — さしみていしょく (sashimi teishoku): a sashimi set meal. 定食 (teishoku) is the key word: it means a fixed set — main dish, rice, miso soup, and pickles on one tray — usually the best-value thing on a lunch menu.

Reading strategy: even when you can't read every kanji, menus repeat a small cast of characters — 席 (seat), 定食 (set meal), 丼 (don, rice bowl), 焼 (yaki, grilled). Learn those ten or so and restaurant Japanese opens up fast.
Why is it 一本 for a bottle of beer but 一枚 for a train ticket? English just says "one".

Japanese counts objects with counters that match the object's shape or category:

- 本 (hon) — long, thin, cylindrical things: bottles, pens, umbrellas, trees, even trains and phone calls historically. 一本のビール = one bottle of beer.
- 枚 (mai) — flat, thin things: tickets, paper, shirts, plates. 一枚の切符 = one ticket.
- 台 (dai) — machines and vehicles: 一台の車 = one car.
- 冊 (satsu) — bound things: 一冊の本 = one book.

Watch the sound changes with 本： 一本 is いっぽん (ippon), 三本 is さんぼん (sanbon), 何本 is なんぼん (nanbon) — the counter's initial h mutates after certain numbers.

If you truly can't remember the right counter, the native Japanese numbers with つ (ひとつ、ふたつ) work for almost anything up to ten and nobody will be confused.
I need to email a Japanese client to move Friday's meeting to Monday. Can you write it politely in Japanese?

件名：金曜日のお打ち合わせの日程変更のお願い

○○様

いつもお世話になっております。
誠に申し訳ございませんが、金曜日のお打ち合わせにつきまして、こちらの都合により、月曜日への変更をお願いできないでしょうか。ご都合のよい時間帯をお知らせいただけますと幸いです。
ご迷惑をおかけいたしますが、何卒よろしくお願い申し上げます。

Key phrases to notice:
- «誠に申し訳ございませんが» — the full-strength apology opener for business; すみません is too light here.
- «お願いできないでしょうか» — literally "might I not be able to ask..."; framing the request as a question about possibility is the polite standard.
- «お知らせいただけますと幸いです» — "it would be a blessing if you could let me know"; 幸いです (saiwai desu) is a signature business-softener.
- The apology comes first, the request second — reversing that order sounds demanding in Japanese business culture.
Translate this station announcement into English: まもなく、2番線に東京行きの電車がまいります。黄色い線の内側でお待ちください。

"A train bound for Tokyo will shortly arrive at platform 2. Please wait behind the yellow line."

Announcement vocabulary that repeats in every Japanese station:
- まもなく (mamonaku) — shortly, in a moment; the standard opener
- ○番線 (bansen) — platform/track number
- 東京行き (Tookyoo-yuki) — bound for Tokyo; 行き (yuki) attaches to any destination
- まいります (mairimasu) — the humble verb for coming/arriving, used because the train "comes" to you
- 内側 (uchigawa) — the inside; «黄色い線の内側» is always the safe side of the platform line
たら, ば, と, なら — Japanese has FOUR words for "if"?! Give me a rule of thumb I can actually use.

Four forms, but one workhorse. Start here:

- たら — the all-purpose "if/when". 雨が降ったら、行きません。(If it rains, I won't go.) Use this by default; it covers most situations, past and future.
- と — automatic, natural consequences; if A happens, B always follows. 春になると、花が咲きます。(When spring comes, the flowers bloom.) Only for things that inevitably follow — never for wishes or requests after it.
- ば — formal, hypothetical, proverb-flavored. 急がば回れ。(More haste, less speed — literally "if you hurry, go the long way round".) Common in writing and set phrases.
- なら — "if it's about X / if what you say is true". 東京へ行くなら、新幹線が便利です。(If you're going to Tokyo, the shinkansen is convenient.) It reacts to a topic or something just mentioned.

Rule of thumb: speak with たら, recognize the others. You'll sound natural 95% of the time, and the remaining 5% is mostly set expressions you'll absorb by listening.
すみません、駅前ホテルまでお願いします。
かしこまりました。駅前ホテルですね。ほかに寄るところはございますか。
途中のコンビニで少し止めてもらえますか。
はい、大丈夫ですよ。では、出発いたします。シートベルトをお締めください。
Correct my Japanese: この本は面白いでした。

One fix: この本は面白かったです。
(Kono hon wa omoshirokatta desu. — This book was interesting.)

The reason: 面白い is an i-adjective, and i-adjectives conjugate THEMSELVES — 面白い → 面白かった (was interesting), 面白くない (isn't interesting). You never add でした to an i-adjective, because the past tense is already inside the word. Adding です after 面白かった is just politeness polish.

Contrast with na-adjectives and nouns, which do use でした: 静かでした (was quiet), 学生でした (was a student). The classic learner error is treating every adjective like a noun — check whether it ends in い that belongs to the adjective itself.
Why are コンビニ, アルバイト and マンション written in katakana? And why does マンション not mean "mansion"?

Katakana is the script for loanwords, and all three are borrowed — but not all from English:

- コンビニ (konbini) — clipped from "convenience store"; Japanese loves shortening long loans to four morae.
- アルバイト (arubaito) — from German «Arbeit» (work), via students in the Meiji era; it means a part-time job, and the worker is often just called バイト.
- マンション (manshon) — from "mansion", but in Japanese it means an ordinary apartment or condo in a concrete building. A real mansion is 豪邸 (goutei) or 大邸宅.

These shifted-meaning loans are called 和製英語's cousins — words that look English but aren't. Other classics: マンション's neighbor アパート (apaato, a smaller/older apartment block), ホッチキス (hotchkiss = stapler, from a brand name), and コンセント (konsento = electrical outlet, from "concentric plug"). Trust the Japanese meaning, not the English echo.
My textbook throws around 尊敬語, 謙譲語 and 丁寧語. What are these three, and how much do I actually need?

Japanese politeness has three separate systems, and they point in different directions:

1. 丁寧語 (teineigo) — polite language. The です/ます style. It polishes YOUR speech in general, toward anyone. You already need this daily.
2. 尊敬語 (sonkeigo) — respectful language. It RAISES the other person's actions: 言う (say) → おっしゃる, 食べる → 召し上がる, 行く → いらっしゃる. Used for customers, teachers, bosses.
3. 謙譲語 (kenjougo) — humble language. It LOWERS your own actions: 言う → 申す, 行く → 参る, する → いたす. Used when you or your group act toward someone you respect.

The logic: respect is relative motion — push them up, push yourself down, never mix the directions (never use sonkeigo for your own actions).

How much do you need? 丁寧語 always. A survival set of the others covers 90% of life: いらっしゃる (be/go/come, respectful), おっしゃる (say), ご覧になる (look), and for yourself 申す, 参る, いたす, plus the all-purpose ございます. Full keigo fluency is a professional skill even native speakers train for — call-center staff take courses in it.
Translate into Japanese, for a guesthouse notice: "Please take off your shoes at the entrance and use the slippers provided."

玄関で靴を脱いで、備え付けのスリッパをご利用ください。
(Genkan de kutsu o nuide, sonaetsuke no surippa o go-riyou kudasai.)

Two details: 玄関 (genkan) is the entryway — the sunken step where shoes come off in every Japanese home and traditional inn; there is no exact English word because the custom itself is built into the architecture. And «ご利用ください» (please use) is the polite notice-style imperative you'll see on signs everywhere, softer than a direct command. The slippers are for the wooden floors only — you'll find a separate pair for the toilet, which is the detail that catches every first-time visitor.
すみません、オーツミルクのラテはありますか。
はい、ございます。サイズはトールとグランデがございますが、いかがなさいますか。
トールでお願いします。あと、パソコン用の電源はありますか。
窓側のお席にコンセントがございます。お会計は四百八十円です。ありがとうございます。
すみません, ごめんなさい, 申し訳ありません — three ways to say sorry? When do I use which?

They form a ladder of weight:

- ごめんなさい (gomen nasai) — the personal apology, for friends and family. Light to medium. Never use it to a customer or a boss — it sounds childish in formal settings.
- すみません (sumimasen) — the all-rounder. It's an apology, an "excuse me" for getting attention, AND a thank-you when someone does you a small favor (holding a door). Medium weight, safe almost everywhere.
- 申し訳ありません (moushiwake arimasen) — the heavy, formal apology: "there is no excuse". Business mistakes, customer complaints, anything with real consequences. Often strengthened to 誠に申し訳ございません.

The classic trap: すみません comes from 済む (to be settled) — "my debt is not settled" — which is why it doubles as thanks: you've put someone out, and the account isn't square. Once you hear it that way, its three jobs stop looking like separate meanings.
Hindi has आप, तुम and तू for "you". My app teaches all three with no guidance. How do I choose without offending anyone?

Hindi politeness is a three-step ladder, and the verb changes with each step:

- आप (aap) — respectful. Elders, strangers, officials, your boss, anyone you'd call "sir/ma'am". Verb is plural-form: आप कहाँ जाते हैं？ (Where are you going?)
- तुम (tum) — familiar. Friends, people your age or younger, family in most homes. तुम कहाँ जाते हो？
- तू (tuu) — intimate or subordinate. Very close friends, small children, in prayer to God — and in anger. तुम कहाँ जाता है？ sounds either deeply affectionate or insulting; learners should simply not use it.

Default to आप with every adult stranger. It can sound slightly formal with a young shopkeeper, but it never offends. People will often invite you down the ladder: «आप तुम कह सकते हो» — until then, stay on the top rung.

Translate this leave application into formal Hindi: "Respected Sir, I respectfully request two days of leave, on 5 and 6 December, due to a family function. I will complete my pending work before leaving. Please grant me leave."

आदरणीय महोदय,

सविनय निवेदन है कि मुझे एक पारिवारिक कार्यक्रम के कारण 5 और 6 दिसंबर को दो दिन का अवकाश चाहिए। जाने से पहले मैं अपना सारा लंबित कार्य पूरा कर दूँगा। कृपया मुझे अवकाश प्रदान करने की कृपा करें।

भवदीय

(Aadarniiya mahodaya, savinay nivedan hai ki mujhe ek paarivaarik kaaryakram ke kaaran 5 aur 6 December ko do din kaa avkaash chaahiye...)

Formal Hindi letters run on set formulas: «सविनय निवेदन है कि» (it is humbly submitted that) opens almost every request, and «भवदीय» (yours faithfully, literally "your [servant]") closes it. These aren't optional decorations — an Indian office letter without them reads as abrupt.
I'm learning Devanagari and hit words like क्षमा and त्रिपाठी. Those stacked letters stop me cold. How do I read them?

Those are conjunct letters (संयुक्ताक्षर) — two consonants fused into one shape. There are three famous ones to learn first, because they have special forms:

- क्ष = क + ष, pronounced "ksh": क्षमा (kshamaa, forgiveness)
- त्र = त + र, pronounced "tr": त्रिपाठी (Tripaathii, a surname), मित्र (mitra, friend)
- ज्ञ = ज + ञ, pronounced "gy" in Hindi: ज्ञान (gyaan, knowledge)

For all other combinations the rule is mechanical: the first consonant loses its right stem and leans into the second — क्त, द्व, स्व (as in स्वागत, welcome). Strategy: learn क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ by sight, then read the rest by spotting which consonant kept its full shape (that's the one pronounced last). The headline (शिरोरेखा) across the top never breaks, so read the bodies hanging below it.
Correct my Hindi: मैं बाज़ार गया और सब्ज़ियाँ खरीदे।

The second half needs two changes:

मैं बाज़ार गया और मैंने सब्ज़ियाँ खरीदीं।
(Main baazaar gayaa aur mainne sabziyaan khariidiin. — I went to the market and bought vegetables.)

What's happening: in the past tense of a transitive verb, Hindi flips its grammar (the ergative pattern). The subject takes ने (main → mainne), and the verb stops agreeing with the subject and agrees with the OBJECT instead. सब्ज़ियाँ is feminine plural, so the verb must be खरीदीं — not खरीदे (masculine plural).

Your first clause was perfect because जाना (to go) is intransitive: no ने, and गया agrees with you. The flip only happens with a direct object in the perfective past.
भैया, कनॉट प्लेस चलोगे? कितने पैसे लगेंगे?
चलिए साहब, बैठिए। मीटर से चलूँगा, करीब डेढ़ सौ रुपये लगेंगे।
मीटर से ठीक है, लेकिन रास्ते में एटीएम पर दो मिनट रुकना है।
कोई बात नहीं, रुक जाऊँगा। आप आराम से बैठिए, मैं छोटा रास्ता लेता हूँ, ट्रैफ़िक कम मिलेगा।
Why is it राम ने खाना खाया but राम खाना खाता था? Where does this ने come from and why does it vanish?

ने is the ergative marker, and Hindi uses it under exactly two conditions, both required:

1. The verb is TRANSITIVE (it has a direct object — खाना, food).
2. The tense is PERFECTIVE (the action is completed — खाया, ate).

When both hold: राम ने खाना खाया। The subject takes ने， and the verb agrees with the object instead — खाना is masculine singular, so खाया.

When either condition fails, no ने：
- Habitual past (not perfective): राम खाना खाता था। — Ram used to eat food. Verb agrees with राम again.
- Intransitive perfective (no object): राम सोया। — Ram slept. No ने possible.

Think of it as Hindi temporarily re-wiring the sentence around the completed act: once an action is done and something has been acted upon, the doer steps back grammatically and the result takes the spotlight. It's the same pattern you'll meet in Punjabi, Marathi, and Nepali.
Translate this into English: अगर मेहनत सच्ची हो, तो सफलता एक दिन ज़रूर मिलती है।

"If the hard work is sincere, success will surely come one day."

(Agar mehnat sachchii ho, to safaltaa ek din zaruur miltii hai.)

Notes on the pieces: अगर...तो is the if...then frame (तो here is the "then" partner, not the emphasis particle). सच्ची literally means "true/genuine" — applied to मेहनत (effort) it means effort that's honest and wholehearted, not just long hours. And ज़रूर (surely, without fail) carries a tone of reassurance: this sentence is something you say to encourage someone who's doubting whether effort pays off.
नमस्ते, मुझे आपका दो कमरों वाला फ्लैट देखना है। किराया कितना है?
नमस्ते! किराया अठारह हज़ार रुपये महीना है, और दो महीने की सिक्योरिटी जमा होगी। फ्लैट तीसरी मंज़िल पर है, लिफ्ट भी है।
क्या मैं इस शनिवार को फ्लैट देखने आ सकता हूँ?
बिल्कुल, शनिवार को सुबह ग्यारह बजे आ जाइए। मैं वहीं मिलूँगा। अपना फ़ोन नंबर दे दीजिए, ताकि मैं पता भेज सकूँ।
Correct my Hindi: मुझे एक किताब चाहिए है।

Drop the है: मुझे एक किताब चाहिए। (Mujhe ek kitaab chaahiye. — I need/want a book.)

चाहिए is a special form that already contains its own "is needed" meaning — it never takes है after it, in the same way English "must" doesn't take "is" ("I must is go" ✗). It's an invariant word: मुझे किताब चाहिए, हमें समय चाहिए, उसे पैसे चाहिए — चाहिए never changes shape no matter who needs what.

The other classic trap in the same family: obligation. "I have to go home" is मुझे घर जाना है — the person goes in the को-form (मुझे), the verb stays an infinitive (जाना), and है agrees with the action, not with you.
Translate this product description into Hindi: "This stainless steel water bottle keeps drinks cold for 24 hours and fits in a standard cup holder."

यह स्टेनलेस स्टील की पानी की बोतल पेय को 24 घंटे तक ठंडा रखती है और सामान्य कप होल्डर में आसानी से आ जाती है।

(Yah stainless steel kii paanii kii botal pey ko 24 ghante tak thandaa rakhtii hai aur saamaanya cup holder mein aasaanii se aa jaatii hai.)

Translation notes: product Hindi freely borrows English technical terms — स्टेनलेस स्टील and कप होल्डर stay in English (in Devanagari dress) because that's how Indian packaging actually reads; a "pure" Hindi word for cup holder would sound artificial. But the verbs go fully Hindi: रखती है (keeps) is feminine because बोतल is feminine, and आ जाती है (fits/comes into) is the natural idiom for fitting into a space.
Why does my Hindi teacher say पिताजी आ रहे हैं with a plural verb? My grandfather is one person. Is it a mistake?

Not a mistake — it's respect built into the grammar. Hindi marks honor by using PLURAL verb forms for a respected singular person:

- पिताजी आ रहे हैं। — Father is coming. (रहे हैं is plural.)
- गुरुजी बैठे हैं। — The teacher is seated.
- आप कैसे हैं？ — How are you? (हैं, plural, for one person addressed as आप.)

The same logic runs through आप itself: आप historically patterns with plurals, which is exactly why it feels respectful. Using the singular form for an elder — पिताजी आ रहा है — would sound like talking about a child or a servant.

English once had a shadow of this: "you" was originally the plural, and it drove out singular "thou" precisely because plural felt politer. Hindi just kept the system fully alive.
भाई साहब, मुझे जयपुर के लिए कल सुबह की दो टिकट चाहिए।
कल सुबह छह बजे वाली गाड़ी में सीट खाली है। दो टिकट के कुल नौ सौ रुपये होंगे। नाम बता दीजिए।
नाम राहुल वर्मा। गाड़ी किस प्लेटफ़ॉर्म से जाएगी?
प्लेटफ़ॉर्म नंबर तीन से। आपकी टिकट तैयार है — यात्रा से आधा घंटा पहले स्टेशन आ जाइएगा। शुभ यात्रा!
I'm learning the Arabic script and مكتبة confuses me — the letters look different from the alphabet chart. How do I read it?

مكتبة is pronounced "maktaba" and means library or bookshop. Your confusion is the central fact of Arabic script: most letters have up to four shapes — alone, at the start, in the middle, and at the end of a word — because letters join like handwriting.

Break مكتبة down right to left:
- م (miim) in initial form: مـ
- ك (kaaf) in middle form: ـكـ
- ت (taa) in middle form: ـتـ
- ب (baa) in middle form: ـبـ
- ة (taa marbuuta) in final form: ـة — this special letter only appears at the end of words and signals a feminine noun; it's pronounced "a" in pause and "at" when linked to what follows.

The skeleton never changes — م is always the little circle with a tail — only the joining strokes stretch. Learn to recognize each letter's "core" and the four shapes become one letter in four poses.
Translate this business email into Arabic: "I would like to invite you to a meeting on Tuesday at 10 a.m. to discuss the new project. Please confirm your attendance."

يسرّني أن أدعوكم إلى اجتماع يوم الثلاثاء في تمام الساعة العاشرة صباحًا لمناقشة المشروع الجديد. أرجو تأكيد حضوركم.

(Yasurrunii an ad'uukum ilaa ijtimaa'in yawm ath-thulaathaa' fii tamaam as-saa'a al-'aashira sabaaHan li-munaaqashat al-mashruu' al-jadiid. Arjuu ta'kiid Huduurikum.)

Formal notes: يسرّني أن (it pleases me to...) is the standard courteous opener for invitations — much warmer than a bare أريد (I want). And في تمام الساعة العاشرة (at exactly ten o'clock) is the fixed formal way to give a time; everyday speech would just say الساعة عشرة.
Correct my Arabic: الطلاب يكتب الدرس. My teacher underlined the verb.

The verb must agree with its plural subject: الطلاب يكتبون الدرس.
(Aṭ-ṭullaabu yaktubuuna ad-darsa. — The students are writing the lesson.)

In Modern Standard Arabic, when the subject comes FIRST (as here), the verb agrees with it fully — الطلاب is plural, so the verb takes the plural ending ـون (yaktubuuna). Your يكتب is the singular form.

There's a twist you'll meet in classical texts: when the verb comes first, it stays singular even with a plural subject — يكتب الطلابُ الدرسَ is also correct classical grammar. But subject-first with full agreement, as in your sentence, is the safe modern standard, and it's what news and formal writing use.
مساء الخير! عندي حجز باسم خالد منصور. هل يمكن أن أحصل على غرفة تطل على النيل؟
مساء النور يا أستاذ خالد! نعم، عندنا غرفة فاضية في الدور الخامس بتطل على النيل. الإفطار من الساعة سبعة لتسعة في المطعم.
ممتاز. وهل فيه واي فاي في الغرفة؟
أيوه، الواي فاي مجاني في كل الغرف، وكلمة السر هتلاقيها على المكتب. لو احتجت أي حاجة، كلمنا في الاستقبال. إجازة سعيدة!
How can كتب mean three different things? My dictionary lists kataba, kutiba and kutub for the same letters.

Because Arabic writes consonants and usually leaves the short vowels out. The letters ك ت ب are a skeleton — the root k-t-b, everything to do with writing — and the vowels you drape over it decide the word:

- كَتَبَ (kataba) — he wrote
- كُتِبَ (kutiba) — it was written (passive: the u-i pattern)
- كُتُب (kutub) — books (plural)

The little vowel marks have names: ًفتحة fatḥa (a), ضمة ḍamma (u), كسرة kasra (i), written above or below the letter. Fully voweled text (tashkeel) appears in the Quran, children's books, poetry, and dictionaries — everywhere else, readers supply vowels from context, which is less impossible than it sounds: the root-and-pattern system means كتب in a sentence about a student can really only be kataba.

Practical tip: when you look a word up, learn it WITH its vowels as one sound — "kataba", not "k-t-b".
Translate this product label into English: يُحفظ في مكان بارد وجاف. صالح لمدة ستة أشهر من تاريخ الإنتاج. يُرجى قراءة التعليمات قبل الاستخدام.

"Store in a cool, dry place. Valid for six months from the date of production. Please read the instructions before use."

Label Arabic has its own clipped register: يُحفظ (yuḥfaẓ, "is to be stored") is a passive imperative — the standard formula on packaging, like English "keep refrigerated" but grammatically a passive verb. صالح لمدة (ṣaaliḥ li-muddat...) literally means "good for a period of..." and is how shelf life is stated; expiry dates themselves are usually printed as تاريخ الانتهاء. Once you know these three formulas, most Arabic packaging is readable.
من فضلك، عايز أروح المطار. هياخد وقت قد إيه؟
تمام، المطار في الظروف العادية بياخد حوالي أربعين دقيقة، بس دلوقتي في زحمة. هتكون الأجرة حوالي ميتين جنيه بالمتر.
تمام، بس سوّق على مهلك لو سمحت، معايا شنط تقيلة ورا.
ما تقلقش، هوصّلك في المعاد. الشنط بأمان في الشنطة ورا. رحلة سعيدة إن شاء الله!
My Arabic grammar book has a whole chapter on "the dual". English doesn't have this. What is it?

Arabic has three numbers, not two: singular, DUAL (exactly two), and plural (three or more). The dual is a full grammatical form, المثنى, used constantly:

- كتاب (kitaab, a book) → كتابان (kitaabaan, two books) → كتب (kutub, books)
- في المدرسة (in the school) → في المدرستين (fii al-madrasatayn, in the two schools)

Formation: add ـان (-aan) in the nominative, ـين (-ayn) in the genitive and accusative. So «two eyes» is عينان, «two days» is يومان.

It applies to nouns, adjectives, pronouns (هما = the two of them), and even verbs (يكتبان = the two of them write). English lost its dual a thousand years ago (Old English had wit, "we two"); Arabic kept it fully alive, so any pair — two hands, two meetings, two brothers — triggers it automatically.
When do I say السلام عليكم versus just مرحبا? And what do I answer?

السلام عليكم (as-salaamu 'alaykum, "peace be upon you") is the full, respectful greeting — appropriate for elders, formal situations, entering a shop or office, and anyone you don't know. It is never wrong.

The reply is fixed: وعليكم السلام (wa 'alaykum as-salaam, "and upon you peace"). Not answering, or answering with a plain hello, is noticeably rude — the reply is part of the greeting.

مرحبا (marhaban) is lighter — a friendly "hello" among peers, younger people, and casual encounters; أهلاً وسهلاً (ahlan wa sahlan) is its warmer cousin, roughly "you've come to family and ease". Time greetings also work everywhere: صباح الخير (ṣabaaḥ al-khayr, good morning) answered by صباح النور (ṣabaaḥ an-nuur, "morning of light").

Rule of thumb: open with السلام عليكم when in doubt; downgrade to مرحبا only once the other person does.
Translate into Arabic for an office form: "Please fill in this form in capital letters and sign at the bottom of the page."

يرجى ملء هذا النموذج بأحرف كبيرة والتوقيع في أسفل الصفحة.

(Yurjaa mal' haadhaa an-namuudhaj bi-aHruf kabiira wa at-tawqii' fii asfal aṣ-ṣafHa.)

Form Arabic relies on a few formulas: يرجى (yurjaa, "it is requested that...") is the universal polite instruction opener — softer than an imperative and standard on every official document. ملء (mal', filling) is the verbal noun of "to fill", and نموذج (namuudhaj) is the word for a form/template. Note that "capital letters" is rendered literally (بأحرف كبيرة) even though Arabic script has no capitals — the phrase survives on bilingual forms for the Latin-alphabet fields.
Why does كتاب الطالب mean "the student's book" when only كتاب has no "the" on it? Definiteness seems backwards.

You've found the iḍāfa (إضافة) — the possessive chain, Arabic's most important construction. Two nouns are chained: كتاب الطالب (kitaab aṭ-ṭaalib).

The rule that feels backwards: the FIRST noun never takes ال (the) — its definiteness comes from the second noun. Because الطالب is definite (the student), the whole chain is definite: THE student's book. If the second noun were indefinite — كتاب طالب (a student's book) — the whole chain is indefinite.

More examples:
- باب البيت (baab al-bayt) — the door of the house
- سيارة المدير (sayyaarat al-mudiir) — the director's car
- مفتاح السيارة (miftaaḥ as-sayyaara) — the key of the car

Chains can stack: مفتاح سيارة المدير — the key of the director's car, with definiteness decided by the very last noun. And watch the ة: in a chain, تاء مربوطة is pronounced "t" — سيارة المدير is sayyaarat al-mudiir, not sayyaara.
السلام عليكم! عايز أشتري هدية لأمي، ممكن تساعدني؟
وعليكم السلام، أهلاً بيك! عندنا شالات حرير جميلة وعطور عربية. أمك بتحب الألوان الفاتحة ولا الغامقة؟
بتحب الأزرق. الشال الأزرق ده بكام؟
ده بتلتمية وخمسين، وهو حرير طبيعي. لو تحب، أغلفهولك هدية من غير زيادة. هتفرح بيه جداً إن شاء الله!
Translate this business email into Italian: "Dear Mr. Rossi, We confirm that your order was shipped today. The invoice is attached. Delivery is expected within three working days."

Gentile Dott. Rossi,

Le confermiamo che il Suo ordine è stato spedito oggi. In allegato trova la fattura. La consegna è prevista entro tre giorni lavorativi.

Cordiali saluti

Business conventions at work: Italian emails address the recipient with a title — «Gentile Dott. Rossi» — even when the person isn't literally a doctor; graduates are routinely addressed as Dottore/Dottoressa. The formal "you" is Lei, written with a capital L in careful correspondence («Le confermiamo», «il Suo ordine»), and the verb agrees in the third person: it is «trova» (he/she finds), not «trovi».
Buongiorno, vorrei due biglietti per Bologna, per domani mattina.
Buongiorno! C'è un treno alle 8:15 con arrivo alle 10:40, oppure uno alle 9:30. Preferisce solo andata o andata e ritorno?
Andata e ritorno, torniamo domenica sera. Si possono cambiare i biglietti, se serve?
Sì, con questa tariffa il cambio è gratuito fino alla partenza. Ecco i biglietti: binario 6. Buon viaggio!
Correct my Italian: "Io ho andato a Roma ieri con i miei amici."

The auxiliary is wrong: «Io sono andato a Roma ieri con i miei amici.»

Italian past tenses choose between two helpers: avere (to have) for most verbs, and essere (to be) for verbs of movement, arrival, staying, and change of state — andare, venire, arrivare, partire, restare, diventare. When essere is the helper, the participle also agrees with the subject: sono andato (a man), sono andata (a woman), siamo andati (a group).

Memory hook: if the verb answers "where did the subject end up?", it probably takes essere. DR MRS VANDERTRAMP is the classic mnemonic list English-speaking students use, but the movement/change logic covers nearly all of it.
When do Italians use «Lei» instead of «tu»? And why does my phrasebook write it with a capital L?

«Lei» is the formal you — grammatically the third person "she", borrowed for politeness centuries ago. You use it with strangers, elders, officials, doctors, clients, and in almost every service encounter where you want to be correct rather than chummy: «Lei desidera?» (What would you like?)

Because it's third person, the verb changes: «Tu hai» becomes «Lei ha»; «il tuo» becomes «il Suo». In formal writing Lei and Suo are capitalized so the reader knows it's an address form and not an actual "she" — in modern informal writing the capitals are often dropped.

Italians switch to tu quickly among the young, but the switch is a small social event: «Possiamo darci del tu?» (Shall we use tu with each other?). Until someone offers, stay with Lei — being too formal for an hour costs nothing; being too familiar in the first minute can cost the relationship.
Translate this museum notice into English: «Il museo è aperto tutti i giorni dalle 9 alle 19. L'ultimo ingresso è alle 18. I biglietti possono essere acquistati anche online.»

"The museum is open every day from 9 a.m. to 7 p.m. Last admission is at 6 p.m. Tickets can also be purchased online."

Two Italian formulas worth stealing: «dalle 9 alle 19» uses the plural article (dalle/alle) because hours are feminine plural (le ore) — you'll see this pattern on every opening-hours sign in Italy. And «l'ultimo ingresso» (the last entry) is the fixed phrase for last admission; museums everywhere phrase the closing rule this way rather than saying when you must leave.

Translate this product description into Italian: "This handmade leather bag is crafted in Florence from full-grain Tuscan leather. It features a cotton lining, an inner zip pocket, and an adjustable strap."

«Questa borsa in pelle fatta a mano è realizzata a Firenze con pelle toscana pieno fiore. È dotata di fodera in cotone, tasca interna con cerniera e tracolla regolabile.»

Craft vocabulary to notice: «pieno fiore» is the exact trade term for full-grain (literally "full flower" — the uncorrected surface of the hide), and Italian product copy prefers «è dotata di» (it is equipped with) over a plain "ha" when listing features. «Fatta a mano» (handmade) conventionally comes right after the product name, where Italian buyers look for it first.
Buonasera, vorrei prenotare un tavolo per quattro persone, per sabato sera.
Buonasera! Per sabato ho disponibilità alle 20:00 o alle 21:30. Quale orario preferisce?
Alle 20:00 va bene. È possibile avere un tavolo in un angolo tranquillo?
Certamente, Le segno un tavolo vicino alla finestra, è la zona più tranquilla. A che nome prenoto?
Correct my Italian: "Le ragazze ha comprato i biglietti ieri."

The verb must be plural: «Le ragazze hanno comprato i biglietti ieri.» (The girls bought the tickets yesterday.)

«Le ragazze» is a plural subject, so the auxiliary is «hanno» (they have), not «ha» (he/she has). The participle «comprato» stays unchanged here because comprare takes avere — participle agreement with the subject is only required with essere verbs (Le ragazze sono arrivate).

Quick check that catches this error: before writing ha/hai/hanno, say the subject aloud. If you could replace it with "they", the answer is always hanno.
I'm learning Hangul and 감사합니다 looks like a wall of blocks. How do I take it apart?

Every Korean syllable is one block made of 2–4 letters packed into a square. 감사합니다 (gamsahamnida, "thank you") has five blocks — read each one separately:

- 감 (gam) = ㄱ (g) + ㅏ (a) + ㅁ (m, the final consonant at the bottom, called batchim)
- 사 (sa) = ㅅ (s) + ㅏ (a)
- 합 (ham) = ㅎ (h) + ㅏ (a) + ㅂ (b/p, which sounds like m before the next block)
- 니 (ni) = ㄴ (n) + ㅣ (i)
- 다 (da) = ㄷ (d) + ㅏ (a)

The recipe never changes: a block starts with a consonant on the left or top, the vowel sits right or below, and an optional final consonant (batchim) goes underneath. Once you can split blocks into their 2–4 parts, any Korean word — signs, menus, names — becomes readable in a few weeks of practice. Hangul was designed in 1443 to be learnable in days, and it genuinely is.
My Korean course mentions 합쇼체, 해요체 and 반말. What are these levels and which one should I live in?

Korean verbs wear their social relationship on their sleeve. The three levels you'll meet daily:

- 합쇼체 (formal polite): 집에 갑니다. — announcements, presentations, news, the military, very formal business. Stiff and distant.
- 해요체 (polite informal): 집에 가요. — the default for adult life: strangers, colleagues, shop staff, most conversations. Warm but respectful.
- 반말 (plain/casual): 집에 가. — close friends, family, children, partners. Using it upward is a genuine insult.

Live in 해요체. It's the safe middle: correct with your boss's boss and kind with a barista. You'll hear 합쇼체 endings (입니다, 갑니다) constantly in media and service formulas — recognize them, answer in 해요체. 반말 will arrive on its own when a Korean friend starts using it to you and invites you to match; that's a small milestone of closeness.
Translate this business email into Korean: "Dear Mr. Kim, Thank you for meeting with us yesterday. We will send you the proposal by Friday."

김 부장님께,

안녕하십니까. 어제 회의에 참석해 주셔서 감사합니다. 제안서는 금요일까지 보내 드리겠습니다.

(Gim bujangnimkke, annyeonghasimnikka. Eoje hoeuie chamseokhae jusyeoseo gamsahamnida. Jeanseoneun geumyoilkkaji bonae deurigessseumnida.)

Business conventions: Korean emails address people by title, not name alone — 김 부장님 (Manager Kim), never just 김 씨 in a formal mail. And note 드리겠습니다: 드리다 is the humble "give" verb used when giving TO someone senior, so "we will send you" becomes a small act of deference built into the verb itself.
안녕하세요, 아이스 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요. 너무 달지 않게 해 주세요.
네, 아이스 아메리카노 한 잔이요. 매장에서 드시고 가세요, 아니면 포장이세요?
매장에서 마실 거예요. 콘센트 있는 자리가 있나요?
네, 창가 자리에 콘센트 있어요. 음료 준비되면 진동벨로 알려 드릴게요. 감사합니다!
Correct my Korean: 저는 학교를 갑니다.

The particle is wrong: 저는 학교에 갑니다. (Jeoneun hakgyoe gamnida. — I go to school.)

를 marks the thing directly acted on (the object): 책을 읽어요 (I read a book), 밥을 먹어요 (I eat rice). But a destination isn't an object — nothing is being done TO the school — so Korean uses 에, the location/direction particle: 집에 가요 (go home), 서울에 살아요 (live in Seoul), 세 시에 만나요 (meet at 3, 에 also marks time).

Test: ask "am I doing something to it, or going/being at it?" Doing → 을/를. Going or being → 에. Your sentence is the single most common particle error learners make, precisely because English uses "to" invisibly inside "go to school".
Translate this subway announcement into English: 이번 역은 시청, 시청역입니다. 내리시는 문은 왼쪽입니다.

"This station is City Hall, City Hall station. The doors on your left will open."

(Literally the second sentence is "the doors through which you descend are on the left" — 내리시는 is the honorific form of "getting off", because announcements speak respectfully to passengers.)

Announcement patterns worth recognizing by ear: 이번 역은 (this station is...), 다음 역은 (the next station is...), and the transfer formula 갈아타실 분은 (those transferring, please...). The station name is always said twice, slowly — that repetition is your cue to listen.
실례합니다, 경복궁에 가려면 어떻게 가야 돼요?
여기서 지하철 3호선을 타시고 경복궁역에서 내리시면 돼요. 걸어가면 이십 분 정도 걸려요.
입장료는 얼마예요? 한복을 입으면 무료라고 들었어요.
네, 맞아요. 한복을 입고 가시면 무료로 입장하실 수 있어요. 근처에 한복 대여점이 많으니까 한번 입어 보세요!
Why does my Korean textbook use 드시다 instead of 먹다 when talking about my grandfather eating? It's the same action.

Because Korean has a set of honorific verbs that replace the ordinary verb entirely when the SUBJECT is someone respected:

- 먹다 (eat) → 드시다 / 잡수시다 (eat, honorific): 할아버지께서 진지를 드세요. (Grandfather is having a meal — note 진지, the honorific word for a meal, replacing 밥.)
- 자다 (sleep) → 주무시다: 할머니께서 주무세요.
- 있다 (be/stay) → 계시다: 선생님께서 교실에 계세요.

The subject also changes costume: 이/가 becomes 께서, and the verb picks up the honorific infix 시. Three signals — special verb, 께서, 시 — all saying the same thing: the doer is above the speaker.

The mirror rule: never use these for yourself. Saying 제가 먹습니다 is normal; 제가 드십니다 would mean you're honoring yourself, which gets a laugh, not respect.
Translate this product description into Dutch: "This lightweight jacket is waterproof and windproof, with two zip pockets and a removable hood."

«Deze lichtgewicht jas is waterdicht en winddicht, met twee zakken met ritssluiting en een afneembare capuchon.»

Notes: Dutch compounds stack just like German ones — «ritssluiting» (zip closure) and «capuchon» (hood, borrowed from French). And «afneembaar» (removable) is built from af-nemen, "to take off" — Dutch product copy loves these transparent home-made adjectives where English reaches for Latin (detachable). If the jacket were only showerproof, Dutch would say «waterafstotend», and the distinction matters commercially in the Netherlands, for obvious weather reasons.
Goedemiddag! Wij willen graag twee fietsen huren voor één dag.
Goedemiddag! Dat kan. Een gewone fiets is vijftien euro per dag, inclusief twee sloten. Ik heb wel een borg van vijftig euro per fiets nodig.
Prima. Tot hoe laat kunnen we de fietsen terugbrengen?
We zijn open tot zes uur, maar u kunt de fietsen ook 's avonds in de stalling zetten en de sleutel in de brievenbus doen. Fijne dag in Amsterdam!
Correct my Dutch: "Ik heb een boek gekocht gisteren."

The time phrase is in the wrong place: «Ik heb gisteren een boek gekocht.» (I bought a book yesterday.)

Dutch main clauses obey the V2 rule — the conjugated verb (heb) must be the second element — and everything else arranges itself around that frame: time expressions come early in the middle field, and the rest of the verb (gekocht) is parked at the very end. So the skeleton is: Ik — heb — [gisteren een boek] — gekocht.

Your sentence used English order, where "yesterday" can trail at the end. In Dutch that final slot is reserved for the verb's leftovers, so a trailing gisteren sounds broken. A handy pattern for the perfect tense: subject + heb/hebt + TIME + rest + past participle, always in that order.
De or het? Dutch nouns seem to pick their article by coin flip. Is there any strategy at all?

Honest answer first: there is no complete rule, and even Belgians and Dutch people occasionally disagree. But you're not flipping a coin — «de» covers about 75% of nouns, and some categories are reliable:

Always «het»:
- Diminutives: het boekje (the little book), het huisje — every -je word, no exceptions
- Infinitive-nouns: het lezen (reading), het eten (the food/eating)
- Most words ending in -um, -isme, -ment: het museum, het moment

Always «de»:
- All plurals: de boeken, de huizen (even when the singular is het)
- People and professions: de man, de lerares
- Most words ending in -ing, -ij, -heid, -teit: de regering, de vrijheid

Strategy: learn each noun WITH its article as one unit (not «boek» but «het boek»), and when you must guess, guess «de» — you'll be right three times out of four.
When do I use «u» and when «jij» in Dutch? I don't want to sound rude — or like a butler.

The Netherlands is one of Europe's most informal cultures, so the balance is tipped toward «jij» (you, informal): colleagues, shop staff, people your age, and even most bosses get jij within minutes. Nobody thinks you're a butler for using it.

«U» survives in narrower places: elderly strangers, very formal business letters, government and legal settings, and deliberately respectful service («Kan ik u helpen?» from an upscale shop assistant). Some Belgians, especially in Flanders, use u and its cousin gij more generously.

The classic mistake is mixing: «u» with a jij-verb form, or starting an email with «Geachte heer» and switching to je halfway. Pick one register per conversation. And the standard business sign-off is «Met vriendelijke groet» (singular groet in formal mail, groeten in friendly mail) — get that right and the u/jij choice matters half as much.
Help me pronounce Dutch: what's happening in «ui», «ij», and the g in «goedemorgen»?

Three famous sounds, in order of difficulty:

1. «ij» (and its twin «ei», pronounced identically) — a diphthong like the "y" in English "my" but rounder: «fijn» ≈ "fine". It even has its own capital letter: IJsselmeer starts with a two-letter capital.
2. «ui» — the sound English doesn't own. Start with the "ow" of "house" and push your lips forward into a French u: «huis» (house), «ui» itself means onion. Approximate it with "œy" and Dutch ears will forgive you.
3. The «g» — a voiced scrape from the back of the throat, like clearing it gently: «goedemorgen» begins with that growl in the north; in Belgium and the south of the Netherlands it's much softer. If the northern g defeats you, a soft Flemish g is understood everywhere.

And a free bonus: the diminutive -je. «Een kopje koffie» isn't just a small cup — -je softens everything it touches, turning orders into requests: «een biertje» is how you order a beer like a local.
